content.text: Finite-horizon scalar LQR uses backward Riccati recursion. For a scalar discrete plant `x[k+1]=a x[k]+b u[k]`, consider a finite-horizon quadratic objective `Σ(q x[k]²+r u[k]²)+q_f x[N]²` with q and q_f nonnegative and r strictly positive. The optimal unconstrained policy under this exact model is `u[k]=−K[k] x[k]`, obtained from backward scalar Riccati recursion. With `S[N]=q_f`, `K[k]=b S[k+1] a/(r+b² S[k+1])`, `S[k]=q+a² S[k+1]−a b S[k+1]K[k]`. Domain context: 10_finite_horizon_optimal_control_and_constraints.md. A declared model is not a validated hardware controller.

The implemented function returns the gain sequence, cost-to-go coefficients, rollout trace and total cost. It verifies that the simulated quadratic cost agrees with `x0² S[0]` under floating-point tolerance. The casebook demonstrates an unstable open-loop coefficient a=1.1 stabilized over a short finite horizon by chosen gains—but no infinite-horizon certificate or real hardware data follows. content.text: A low quadratic model cost is not evidence of good production control. A true application must handle actuator and state constraints, disturbances, model mismatch, delay and safety barriers. If an unconstrained LQR asks for a physically impossible command, simply clipping it does **not** preserve optimality or the Riccati proof. Model predictive control solves a constrained optimization at each step but requires reliable computation timing and feasibility management. MIT Underactuated Robotics distinguishes unconstrained discrete Riccati methods from these harder constrained variants. Domain context: 10_finite_horizon_optimal_control_and_constraints.md.
